explainers.title: 1. Rules you know
explainers.body: A rule tells us what to do and what not to do. We see rules everywhere. There are rules at school, rules at home, and even rules at the pool in Berbera, like: do not run near the water. Nadia knows lots of rules. Do you? Talk about the rules you know.

explainers.title: 2. Fair or not fair?
explainers.body:
A fair rule is kind for everyone. A rule that is unfair is not kind for everyone. Karim and Leila are sorting these rules. You can too! Read each rule with your grown-up. Put a tick for fair or not fair.

Now talk about your ticks with your grown-up. Why is a rule fair or not fair? Who does a fair rule help? A fair rule is good for everyone, not just for one person.

rows: Everyone gets a turn on the swing.
Only the tallest child is allowed to play.
We put our rubbish in the bin.
You must give me your snack.
We listen when a friend is talking.

explainers.title: 3. Friendship rules
explainers.body:
Friends have rules too, even if we do not write them down! Good friends are kind to each other. Amal and Leila made a list of friendship rules. Here are some of them. Read each one, then put a tick next to the ones you think are good rules for friends.

Nadia likes the rule We take turns. Her friend Amal likes We share. Which one do you like best? Tell your grown-up why.

Draw you and a friend playing together in a fair way.

rows: We take turns.
We share our toys and games.
We say sorry when we are wrong.
We let our friends play with other people too.
We say kind words, not mean words.
Draw two friends playing fairly

explainers.title: 4. Be a rule detective
explainers.body:
Now let's find real rules, just like Nadia did at Ehel Academy! Walk around your school with a grown-up. Look carefully for rules and signs, like Please knock on a door, or Walk, do not run in a hallway. Signs are rules too. Write or draw two rules you find.

How many rules did you find in all? Write the number in the box.

explainers.title: 5. Ask a question
explainers.body: A question helps us find out what people think. When we do not know something, we can ask! Nadia wants to know what children think about the playground rules. So she is going to ask them. Now it is your turn. Write one question you could ask about your school.

explainers.title: 6. Make your own rule
explainers.body:
Now you be the Rule Maker! Think of one fair rule that would help everyone at your school be happy, safe or kind. It could be a rule for the playground, the classroom, or lunch time. Write your rule and draw a sign for it, so everyone can see it.

Tell your grown-up why your rule is fair, and who it helps.

headers: Draw a sign for your rule

bigIdeas.title: Two kinds of question
lines: Open question: people can say anything. Like: What do you think about the playground rules?
Closed question: people pick an answer. Like: Do you feel safe here? Yes or No.

bigIdeas.title: Your polite hello
lines: Hello. My name is ...
I am doing a questionnaire about our school rules.
Do you have time for two questions?
Thank you for your help.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor with your grown-up.
Tell it one rule at your school.
Ask it: Is this a fair rule? Why?
Ask it to help you think of one question to ask about the playground.

Well done, rule detective! You talked about rules, you sorted fair and not fair, you found real rules at school, and you even made a rule of your own. You also wrote your very own question. That is a lot of thinking. In the next part, you will put your questions together and make a whole questionnaire to ask real people. Get ready. It is going to be fun!

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: Tell your AI tutor one thing you found out.
Ask it: What is one way we could make our questionnaire even better next time?
Say thank you and hello to your next Global Perspectives adventure.
You made a questionnaire, asked real people, and showed what you found. You listened, you were fair, and you were a good team member. You are a real Rule Maker and a real researcher. Well done!

Keep this project safe, so you can look at it again. Maybe you can show a teacher what you found, and share your idea for a better rule. That is how researchers help to make things fairer for everyone. Say hello to your next Global Perspectives adventure. We are so proud of you!

grownUpGuide.label: For the grown-up
grownUpGuide.intro: This part is written for the parent or teacher sitting with the learner, and is kept in their own words.

sections.title: Hello, and welcome
sections.body:
Welcome to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This guide is written for you, the teacher or parent who will lead this unit beside your child. Global Perspectives is a little different from other subjects. It is not about learning a long list of facts. It is about learning to think: to ask good questions, to find things out, to listen to other people, and to be fair. This unit is called Rule Makers, and it is all about rules.

Your child is about seven or eight years old, so this unit is short, gentle and full of talking, drawing and doing. You lead the way. You read the pages aloud, ask the simple questions, and do the activities together. You will meet your Ehel Academy teacher about twice a week, and in between you and your child work through the activities at your own pace. There are no tests and no marks here. The goal is a child who feels curious, kind and proud.

sections.title: What your child will learn
sections.body:
In this unit your child grows three big Global Perspectives skills, in a way that fits their age:

These are life skills, not just school skills. A child who can ask a clear question, listen to the answer, and think about what is fair will make good choices for the rest of their life. That is why we begin so young, with something every child already knows a lot about: rules.

You do not need to be a teacher to do this well. Your warmth and your patience matter far more than any special knowledge. When you slow down, listen, and take your child's ideas seriously, you are already teaching Global Perspectives. Everything else in this guide is simply there to help you enjoy it together.
items: Asking questions and finding out. We call this research. Your child learns to ask a simple question and collect people's answers, ending with their very own little questionnaire.
Thinking about fair rules. Your child talks about rules for friends, games and school, and thinks about which rules are fair, and why we have rules at all.
Listening and sharing. We call this communication. Your child learns to say what they think kindly, and to listen when a friend thinks something different.

sections.title: The big idea: Rule Makers
sections.body: Rules are everywhere. There are rules at the swimming pool in Berbera, rules in every game, rules at home, and rules at school. Someone made each of those rules for a reason. In this unit your child becomes a rule detective. They look at rules for friendship, rules for games and rules for school, and they ask the big question: are our rules fair, and could they be better? By the end, your child will help make and ask a simple questionnaire about your school's rules.

sections.title: Meet Nadia
sections.body:
To make each lesson clear, your child follows one friendly character through the whole unit. Her name is Nadia. She is in Year 3 at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa, and she is curious about everything, especially rules. Nadia wonders how many rules her school really has, and whether they are all fair.

Nadia's friends help her find out. There is Karim, who loves games; Amal and Leila, who write friendship rules; Omar, who worries about safety on the road; and Grace, who is new to the school. Nadia even has a friend called Idris who lives far away in Mogadishu, and the two of them sometimes share the rules from their two schools. Your child will enjoy meeting them all.

sections.title: How to teach this unit, the Ehel way
sections.body:
At Ehel Academy, three kinds of help work together for young learners:

A few pages have a warm box that says Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up). These are short, gentle moments where you and your child talk to the tutor as a friendly helper. You might ask it to say a hard word in easy words, to give one example of a fair rule, or to help think of a question. Keep these moments short and enjoy them together.
items: You, the grown-up, leading. You are the most important helper. You read the pages aloud, ask the simple questions, and sit beside your child while they draw, tick and talk. Go slowly, and stop for a rest whenever your child needs one.

Your Ehel Academy teacher, about twice a week. In the live sessions your child shares their favourite work, plays a rule game with other children, and asks the questions that matter most. Bring along whatever your child made that week.

The AI tutor, any time, always with a grown-up. Ehel Academy gives every child a friendly AI tutor. For young children it is used together with you: you read its words aloud and help your child answer back. It is never a screen to leave a young child alone with.

sections.title: Key words for this unit
sections.body: Here are the key words your child will meet. Keep them simple, and do not teach them all at once. They come up naturally, one at a time, inside the lessons.

headers: What it means, in easy words
rows: rule
Something that tells us what we should or should not do.
fair
When something is right and kind for everyone.
unfair
When something is not right or not kind for everyone.
friendship
Being a good friend to someone.
question
Something you ask to find out an answer.
questionnaire
A short list of questions you ask lots of people.
open question
A question where people can give any answer they want.
closed question
A question where people pick from answers you give, like yes or no.
tally chart
A way to count answers using little marks.
pictogram
A chart that uses small pictures to show how many.
introduction
A short, polite hello you say before you ask your questions.

sections.title: What you will need
sections.body: This unit uses simple things you already have:
items: Paper, pencils and crayons for drawing and writing.
The Activity Sheet and the Mini-Project & Reflection files, printed or on a screen.
A safe way to walk around the school (or the home, if you are learning at home) to look for rules.
Sticky notes or a small notebook for making tally marks.
The AI tutor ready, for the few boxes that ask for it.

sections.title: How to run the six lessons
sections.body: Here is how to lead each of the six short lessons. Each one has an Aim (what it is for), a Talk about part (chat together first), and a Do part (the activity). Take about half an hour for each, and split it over two sittings if your child would rather.

sections.title: Lesson 1: Rules about friendship
sections.body:
Aim: Your child talks about what makes a good friend, and sees that friends can have different ideas about the same thing.

Talk about: Ask, hello, what makes someone a good friend? Let your child give three ideas. Then explain that Nadia and her friend Grace each wrote friendship rules. Some were the same and some were different, and that is perfectly fine.

Do: Together, look at two short lists of friendship rules in the Activity Sheet. Which rules are the same? Which are different? Tick or draw the ones you both agree with. You can gently show the idea of two circles that overlap: things that are the same go in the middle. This is a first, simple taste of comparing.

sections.title: Lesson 2: How similar are we?
sections.body:
Aim: Your child finds out that people are similar in some ways and different in others, and starts to count answers.

Talk about: Ask, do you and your best friend like all the same things? Talk about one thing that is the same and one thing that is different. Being different is a good thing, not a problem.

Do: Trace your child's hand on paper and help them write five things about themselves, such as a favourite food, colour and game. Compare with your own, or with a brother, sister or friend. Then make a simple tally chart: put one mark each time someone likes the same thing. This is your child's first taste of collecting and counting answers.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Playing the game
sections.body:
Aim: Your child sees why games need rules, and practises working together kindly.

Talk about: Ask, what happens if we play a game and everyone follows different rules? Talk about a game your child knows well.

Do: Read the rules for a simple board game together, such as Snakes and Ladders, and play one quick round. Then help your child say the rules of a game they know, in their own words, using Players must and Players must not. Along the way, praise good team habits: taking turns, listening, and adding a kind idea.

sections.title: Lesson 4: How many rules does our school have?
sections.body:
Aim: Your child becomes a rule detective and finds the real rules around the school.

Talk about: Ask, how do we know the rules at school? Who made them, and why? Look at your classroom rules together, and at signs such as Please knock or Walk, do not run.

Do: Go on a short rule walk around the school (or around your home) with your child. Look for rules and signs. Draw them or take photos, and make notes. Then count them. Talk about which rule your child would add, and which they would take away. This gentle hunt is real research.

sections.title: Lesson 5: Asking questions
sections.body:
Aim: Your child learns that we can find out what people think by asking, and meets open and closed questions.

Talk about: Tell the story of Nadia noticing a problem: some children were not sure of the playground rules. How could she find out what everyone thinks? Introduce the word questionnaire, a short list of questions for lots of people.

Do: Look at Nadia's example questions together. Sort them into open questions, where people can say anything, and closed questions, where people pick from answers you give. Then practise turning the answers to one closed question into a tally chart. Keep it light and playful.

sections.title: Lesson 6: Making a questionnaire
sections.body:
Aim: Your child chooses good questions and learns to say a short, polite introduction.

Talk about: Ask, if you wanted to ask a teacher some questions, what would you say first? Talk about being polite, saying hello, and saying thank you.

Do: Play a quick question-and-answer game to warm up. Then help your child pick the best questions for a questionnaire, for example about food at school or the playground. Put the introduction words in order together: Hello, my name is, I am doing a questionnaire about, thank you. Practise saying it out loud until it feels easy.

sections.title: Using the AI tutor well, with a grown-up
sections.body: For young children the AI tutor is best used as something you do together, like reading a story. Sit beside your child, read the tutor's words aloud, and let your child do the talking back. Keep each turn short. The tutor is a friendly helper, not a babysitter, so please stay with your child the whole time.

sections.title: The Final task: a school-rules questionnaire
sections.body:
The unit builds towards one small, exciting project. Your child, in a little team of friends or simply with you, will make and ask a short questionnaire about your school's rules. The full child-sized steps are set out in the Mini-Project & Reflection file, but here is the shape of it so you can plan:

Your job is to keep it small, safe and happy. Three or four questions is plenty. Help your child choose who to ask, and stay close by while they ask. Every question your child asks is a real piece of research, so celebrate each one.

The project works whether your child is in a team of friends or working just with you. In a team, help them take turns and share the jobs, so one child asks while another writes the tally marks. On their own, you can be their partner: your child asks the questions and you help them record the answers. Either way, the learning is the same, and the pride at the end is just as big.
items: Choose one place in the school, such as the playground, the lunch room or the library.
Think about the rules in that place, and whether anything could be better.
Write two or three simple questions, with one open question and one closed question.
Say a short, polite introduction before asking.
Ask a few people, such as friends, a teacher or family.
Show the answers in a tally chart or a pictogram, and share what you found.

sections.title: Thinking back: How successful was our questionnaire?
sections.body:
At the very end, help your child look back on the project. For this age, reflection is simple and spoken. Sit together and talk about a few gentle questions: Did our questionnaire help us find out what people think? Were our questions easy to answer? Did we ask enough people? Was our chart clear and easy to see?

Then let your child tell you what they enjoyed most, what was tricky, and who helped them. There is a simple picture checklist in the Mini-Project file to guide this. Remember, there are no marks. A child who feels proud of asking real people real questions has already succeeded.

sections.title: Little tips that make it go well
sections.body:
You know your child best, so trust yourself. These small tips can help the unit feel happy rather than heavy:

If a lesson does not go to plan, that is completely fine. A messy, chatty, joyful hour where your child asked lots of questions is a success, even if nothing got written down. Come back to the page whenever you are both ready.
items: Talk first, write later. For this age, talking is the real learning. Let your child say their ideas out loud before they ever pick up a pencil.
Keep it short. Ten to twenty minutes of happy work beats an hour of tired work. Stop while your child is still enjoying it, and come back later.
Follow their curiosity. If your child gets excited about one rule or one place, go with it. A questionnaire about a topic they love will always go better.
Praise the trying, not just the answer. Say things like, I love how you asked that, or, that was a brave question. Effort is what we are growing.
Make it real. Whenever you can, look at real rules and real signs around you, at home, at school, or at the shops. Real life is the best classroom.

sections.title: A last word
sections.body: Thank you for leading this unit. When you read aloud, ask a question, and wait kindly for your child's answer, you are teaching the most important skills in Global Perspectives just by being there. Enjoy becoming rule detectives together, and we will see you in the next unit.

project.title: Mini-project
project.intro: Hello! This is your big project at Ehel Academy. You will make a short questionnaire about your school's rules, and ask some people what they think. Nadia and her friends Karim, Amal and Grace did this too, and now it is your turn. Do it with your grown-up and, if you can, a small team of friends. Take it one step at a time. You can do it!

steps.title: Choose a place
steps.intro: Pick one place in your school to find out about. It could be the playground, the lunch room, or the library. Choose a place you know well and care about. Nadia's team chose the playground, because that is where they play every day. Write the place you choose in the box.

steps.title: Write your questions
steps.intro: Now write two or three questions about the rules in your place. Try one open question and one closed question. Your grown-up can help you write them.

steps.title: Say a polite hello
steps.intro: Before you ask, say a short, polite hello. This is called your introduction. Read it with your grown-up and practise saying it.

steps.title: Who will you ask?
steps.intro: Decide with your grown-up who to ask. Maybe some friends, a teacher, or your family. Try to ask about five people. Write who you will ask.

steps.title: Ask your questions
steps.intro: Now do your questionnaire! This is the exciting part. Walk up to a person with your grown-up. Say your polite hello. Then ask your questions, one by one, and wait for the answer. Listen carefully to what each person says, and write it down. Your grown-up can help you write. Do not rush. Remember to say thank you at the end. Then find the next person and do it all again.

steps.title: Show what you found
steps.intro:
You have lots of answers now. Let's show them so they are easy to see and count. For a closed question, you can make a tally chart. A tally chart uses little marks. You put one mark for each answer, and then you count the marks. Here is a tally chart Nadia made when she asked, do you feel safe in the playground?

You can also make a pictogram. A pictogram uses little pictures instead of marks. Draw one small picture for each answer. So four happy faces would mean four people said yes! Pick tally marks or a pictogram, whichever you like best, and make your own chart in the box.

rows: Yes
No

steps.title: Share what you found
steps.intro: Now share your work! Tell your class, your team, or your family what you found out. You can hold up your tally chart or pictogram and say: We asked five people. Most of them said ... Speak slowly and clearly, and be proud. You could even say one idea to make a school rule better. Well done. You asked real questions and found real answers. That is exactly what a researcher does!

assessment.note: Stages 1-3 are assessed through the mini-project and the look-back grid; the source pack ships no quiz.

selfAssessment.statement: Our questionnaire helped us find out about our rules.
Our questions were easy to answer.
We had an open question and a closed question.
Our chart was clear and easy to see.
